clauses.reason: The clause approves the Code of Fair Competition for the Fishery Industry, and its effectiveness was stayed for ten days by the separate stay clause: "do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved". The clause depends on the approved code for its effect: under section 3(b) of Title I "provisions of such code shall be the standards of fair competition" for the trade or industry. S.J. Res. 113, approved June 14, 1935, provides in section 2 that "All the provisions of Title I of such Act delegating power to the President to approve or prescribe codes of fair competition and providing for the enforcement of such codes are hereby repealed", so this command had no operative effect after June 14, 1935. The resolution states no deferred effective date (it ends "Approved, June 14, 1935."), and June 16, 1935 is not an end because section 1 replaced the two-year expiry with "April 1, 1936". Schechter (decided May 27, 1935) held the section 3 code-making authority an unconstitutional delegation; that is recorded as a validity characterization and not as an end date.

The clause provides that "provisions thereof shall not become effective and they are hereby stayed for a period of 10 days in order to afford consideration of the objections of any interested parties" and that "at the expiration of which period the said Code shall become effective unless I shall by my further Order otherwise determine or extend such stay". The stay is a fixed ten-day period running from the order of February 26, 1934, so it ended by its own terms. The end is recorded inclusive as March 8, 1934, the tenth day counting February 27, 1934 as the first; on the exclusive reading the stay lapsed at the expiration of March 8 and the code became effective on March 9, 1934, and if the day of signing is counted as the first day the tenth day is March 7. The order reserved a power to extend the stay by further order; no held order does so, so the held evidence supports the own-terms end and shows no extension. The approval clause is a separate command and ends on June 14, 1935 by statutory repeal.

inventory_overrides.reason: The machine inventory treats the approval and the ten-day stay as one clause; the approval (the order that the code be approved) and the stay proviso are separate commands with different ends, so each gets its own scope.
The proviso staying the code's provisions for ten days is a separate operative command from the approval and has its own own-terms end.

research_rationale:
This order is a presidential approval, under section 3 of Title I of the National Industrial Recovery Act, of the Code of Fair Competition for the Fishery Industry: "do order that the said Code of Fair Competition be and it is hereby approved". Its only legal effect depended on that code (NIRA section 3(b) made the code's provisions the standards of fair competition). Congress approved S.J. Res. 113 on June 14, 1935, and section 2 repealed the provisions of Title I that delegated power to approve or prescribe codes and provided for their enforcement, so the approval had no operative effect after that date. Schechter's May 27, 1935 holding that the section 3 delegation was unconstitutional is recorded as a validity characterization and not as an end date, following the reviewed shared analysis. The text relied on is the American Presidency Project transcription, so the original is not yet held and the quotation must be re-checked when an official copy is retrieved.

savings.reason: Acts done and liabilities incurred under the code before June 14, 1935 are accrued effects of the approval. Section 5 of Title I exempted a code approved and in effect under the title, and complying action, from the antitrust laws while the title was in effect "and for sixty days thereafter"; whatever exemption survives for past action is an accrued effect. The proviso to section 2 of S.J. Res. 113 names agreements and action thereunder, not codes, and states no time limit, so the held text does not settle its reach. No held source continues the approval itself after June 14, 1935.
